title: My day, my week
cando: talk about your routine, times and how often you do things

about.text: In this lesson you talk about your day and your week. You say what time you do things and how often you do them. You also read a shift rota. Then you find a time to meet a friend.
goals: Ask and answer: What time do you get up? What do you do on Saturdays?
Say how often: always, usually, never, every Saturday.
Say what other people do: she works, he watches.
Read a shift rota and opening times, and write about your weekday.
Use your rota to agree a time to meet.

chapters.title: What do you do on Saturdays?
chapters.text:
In this lesson you talk about your day and your week.
First, two colleagues talk on a break at work.
They ask: What do you do on Saturdays? What time do you get up?
They also ask: How often do you see her? The answer is: Every Saturday.
Listen for the days of the week, and for the times.
Listen to the end of the verbs too: she works, he watches.

chapters.title: I work, she works
chapters.text:
Now the grammar. For your routine, use the present simple.
I work. You work. We work. They work.
But with he and she, add s. She works. He starts at two.
After ch and sh, add es. He watches. She finishes.
To say how often, use always, usually or never. Put it before the verb: I usually get up at six.
For times, use at with a clock time: at seven o'clock.
Use on with a day: on Monday. Use in with part of the day: in the morning.

chapters.title: A shift rota
chapters.text:
Next, you read a shift rota and the opening times of a supermarket.
A rota shows who works on each day, and when.
Find the names, the days and the times.
Then you write about your weekday, from the morning to the night.

chapters.title: Find a time to meet
chapters.text:
Then you look at your own rota. You find a time to meet a friend.
Say when you are busy: Sorry, I'm on the late shift on Wednesday.
Say when you are free: Thursday is my day off.
At the end, say the day and the time back: Thursday at eleven? Great!

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a short story about a person's day and week.
Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

warmup.prompt: What time do you usually get up on a weekday?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. People on an early shift often get up at five. People on a late shift often get up much later.

conversation.title: On a break at work
conversation.setting: Carlos and Amina work at the same supermarket. They are on a break in the staff room.
lines: Amina, what do you do on Saturdays?
I usually go to the market in the morning.
I have lunch with my sister. She works in an office, so she's free at the weekend.
How often do you see her?
Every Saturday. What about you? Do you work at the weekend?
Yes, I work on Saturdays, but I never work on Sundays.
What time do you get up on Sundays?
Late! At about ten. Then I have a big breakfast.
Does your wife work on Sundays?
Yes, she does. She works at a hospital. She starts at seven in the morning.
So what do you do all day?
I watch TV with my son. He watches football all afternoon!

questions.q: What does Amina usually do on Saturday mornings?
wrong: She has lunch with her sister.
questions.why: Amina says: I usually go to the market in the morning.
Carlos says: I never work on Sundays.

questions.q: What time does Carlos's wife start work on Sundays?
questions.why: Carlos says: She starts at seven in the morning.

phrases.text: What do you do on Saturdays?
What time do you get up?
How often do you see her?

phrases.use: Saying you like what somebody tells you.

items.meaning: The day after Sunday. For many people, the first day of the working week.
items.example: I start work at eight on Monday.

items.meaning: The day after Monday.
items.example: My English class is on Tuesday evening.

items.meaning: The day after Tuesday. You don't say the first d: Wenz-day.
items.example: The bank closes early on Wednesday.

items.meaning: The day after Wednesday. It starts with th, like three.
items.example: Can we meet on Thursday?

items.meaning: The day after Thursday. For many people, the last day of the working week.
items.example: On Friday, I finish work at four.

items.meaning: The day after Friday. It is the first day of the weekend.
items.example: I go to the market on Saturday morning.

items.meaning: The day after Saturday. It is the last day of the weekend.
items.example: Many shops open late on Sunday.

items.meaning: Saturday and Sunday.
items.example: What do you do at the weekend?

items.meaning: To get out of bed in the morning.
items.example: I get up at six on weekdays.

items.meaning: To get into bed at night, to sleep.
items.example: I usually go to bed at eleven.

items.meaning: The food you eat in the morning.
items.example: I have breakfast at seven: tea and toast.

items.meaning: The food you eat in the middle of the day.
items.example: We have lunch at one o'clock.

items.meaning: The food you eat in the evening. For many people, it is the big meal of the day.
items.example: My husband cooks dinner on Fridays.

items.meaning: To sit and look at the television.
items.example: He watches TV after dinner.

sound.title: she works, he watches
sound.explain: After he and she, the verb ends in s. In works, starts and cooks, the s is short. It adds no new part. In watches, washes and finishes, es adds a new part: watch-es. Listen, then say each group.

sayIt.instructions: Say Carlos's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Can you hear the s in works and the es in watches?
lines: Yes, I work on Saturdays, but I never work on Sundays.
Late! At about ten. Then I have a big breakfast.
Yes, she does. She works at a hospital. She starts at seven in the morning.
I watch TV with my son. He watches football all afternoon!

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Some are about Carlos and Amina. Some are about other people.
examples: I usually go to the market in the morning.
spot.question: Look at work and works, and watch and watches. When does the verb end in s or es? Where do usually and never go?
spot.answer: After I, you, we and they: work, watch. After he and she: works, watches. Usually and never go before the verb: I usually go, I never work.

rules.title: Every day: I work, she works
rule: I, you, we, they + verb: I work on Saturdays. We start at eight.
He, she, it + verb + s: She works at a hospital. He starts at two.
Add es after ch, sh, s, x and o: watches, washes, finishes, goes, does.
have → has: She has lunch at one.
No s after does and doesn't: Does she work? She doesn't work.
rules.mistake: Not: She work on Sundays. Say: She works on Sundays.

rules.title: How often and when: always, usually, never · at, on, in
rule: Always, usually, sometimes and never go before the verb: I usually get up at six.
Never already means no: I never work on Sundays.
at + a clock time: at seven o'clock, at half past five. Also: at night, at the weekend.
on + a day: on Monday, on Saturday morning.
in + part of the day: in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening.
rules.mistake: Not: in Monday, on the morning. Say: on Monday, in the morning.

practice.why: She + verb + s: my sister works.
Watch ends in ch, so add es: watches.
A question with he or she: Does she …?
No s after doesn't: she doesn't work.

practice.q: I ___ work on Sundays. Sunday is my day off.
practice.why: It's your day off, so never.

options: I go usually to work by bus.
I usually go to work by bus.
I usually goes to work by bus.
practice.a: I usually go to work by bus.
practice.why: Usually goes before the verb: I usually go.
at + a clock time: at nine o'clock.

practice.q: I usually cook dinner ___ the evening.
practice.why: in + part of the day: in the evening.

yourTurn.prompt: Tell a new colleague about your week. What do you usually do on weekdays and on Saturdays? Say one thing you never do. Then say one thing about a friend or somebody in your family.
yourTurn.model: On weekdays, I usually get up at six and start work at eight. I have lunch at one. On Saturdays, I go to the market in the morning. I never work on Sundays. My brother works in a hotel. He watches TV every evening.

text.title: Hilltop Supermarket: the rota
text.body:
PRACTICE: this shop and these people are not real.

HILLTOP SUPERMARKET
OPENING TIMES
Weekdays: 7 am to 10 pm
Saturday: 8 am to 10 pm
Sunday: 10 am to 4 pm

STAFF SHIFT ROTA
Week starting Monday 9 June
Early shift: 6 am to 2 pm
Late shift: 2 pm to 10 pm
Sunday shift: 9:30 am to 4:30 pm

Monday: Amina early, Carlos late
Tuesday: Amina early, Carlos late
Wednesday: Amina early, Omar late
Thursday: Priya early, Omar late
Friday: Amina early, Carlos late
Saturday: Priya early, Carlos late
Sunday: Omar

Every shift has a 30-minute break.
Saturday is always very busy. Please be on time.
Do you want to change a shift? Ask Mr Novak before 12 o'clock on Thursday.

gist.a: a supermarket's opening times and work rota
gist.why: It shows when the shop is open, and who works each shift.

gist.a: the people who work at the supermarket
gist.why: It says STAFF SHIFT ROTA. It has the names of the people who work there.

detail.q: What time does the shop open on Sunday?
detail.why: Opening times: Sunday: 10 am to 4 pm.

detail.q: What time does Amina finish on Monday?
detail.why: Amina is on the early shift: 6 am to 2 pm.
On Wednesday, Amina and Omar work. Carlos is not on the rota.

items.meaning: The hours you work on one day. Many jobs have an early shift and a late shift.
items.example: I'm on the early shift this week.

items.meaning: A list. It shows who works on each day, and at what time.
items.example: Check the rota for next week.

items.meaning: A short time when you stop work and rest.
items.example: We have a 30-minute break at twelve.

items.meaning: Sixty minutes.
items.example: My shift is eight hours.

items.meaning: A short time. There are sixty minutes in an hour.
items.example: The bus comes every ten minutes.

items.meaning: You say it after a number, for an exact hour. 9:00 is nine o'clock.
items.example: The shop opens at nine o'clock.

items.meaning: Near the start of the day, or before the usual time.
items.example: The early shift starts at six.

items.meaning: Near the end of the day, or after the usual time.
items.example: The late shift finishes at ten at night.

items.meaning: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday or Friday.
items.example: The library opens at nine on weekdays.

items.meaning: With a lot to do, or with a lot of people.
items.example: The shop is very busy on Saturdays.

items.meaning: Not busy: you have time. It can also mean you don't pay.
items.example: Are you free on Thursday evening?

model.title: My weekday
model.body:
I work in a supermarket. This week, I'm on the early shift.
I get up at five o'clock and have a quick breakfast.
I start work at six. My break is at ten, for thirty minutes.
I finish at two, and I have lunch at home.
In the evening, I usually cook dinner and watch TV.
I never go to bed late, because I get up early!

write.task: Write about your weekday, from the morning to the night. Write five or six sentences. Put a time in four sentences. Use always, usually or never one time.
write.starter: On weekdays, I get up at …
checklist: I wrote five or six sentences, from the morning to the night.
I used at with every clock time: at seven o'clock.
I put always, usually or never before the verb.
Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

card.title: Find a time to meet
card.situation: Your friend Lena wants to meet for a coffee this week. You work shifts. You are on the early shift on Monday, Tuesday and Saturday. You are on the late shift on Wednesday and Friday. Thursday and Sunday are your days off.
card.goal: Use your rota. Say when you are busy and when you are free. Then agree a day and a time.

phrases: Sorry, I'm on the late shift on Wednesday.
I start at two and finish at ten.
See you on Thursday at eleven!
prepare.notes: Look at your rota. Write your free days and times. Then write two times you can meet.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher gives you a rota. Your partner has a different one. Find a day and a time when you are both free.
doIt.wehel: You are my friend. You want to meet me for a coffee this week. I work shifts. Ask me when I am free, and suggest two times. I will look at my rota and answer. Agree a day and a time with me. Use simple English.

model.title: When are you free?
lines: Hi! Do you want to meet for a coffee this week?
Yes, good idea! When are you free?
Are you free on Monday evening?
Sorry, Monday is bad. I'm on the early shift, so I go to bed early.
I'm on the late shift on Wednesday. I start at two and finish at ten.
Thursday is my day off. I'm free all day.
Great! Thursday morning, at eleven o'clock?
Thursday at eleven? Yes, that's fine. Where do you want to meet?
The café next to the station?
Perfect. See you on Thursday at eleven!
compare: Did you say when you are busy, and why?
Did you say your start and finish times?
Did you use on, at and in: on Thursday, at eleven, in the morning?
Did you say the day and the time back to check them?

canDo: I can talk about my routine on weekdays and at the weekend.
I can ask: What time do you …? How often do you …?
I can say what other people do: she works, he watches.
I can read a shift rota and opening times.
I can use my rota to agree a time to meet.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first picture. Who is the story about? What time of day is it?
reading.talk: Is the person's week like your week? What is your favourite day of the week, and why? Write two or three sentences, or say them to Wehel.

quiz.why: Watch ends in ch, so add es.

quiz.q: I ___ work on Sundays. It's my day off.
quiz.why: A day off: you never work.

quiz.q: A list of who works on each day is a ___ .
quiz.why: A rota shows who works, and when.

quiz.q: ___ does your shift start? At six o'clock.
quiz.why: The answer is a time, so ask: What time …?

quiz.q: The bag is over there. Can I have ___ one, please?
quiz.why: One thing, not near you: that one.

quiz.q: She ___ speak Spanish, but she can't speak French.
quiz.why: can + verb, with no s and no to.

quiz.q: There ___ two bedrooms in the flat.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the break-time conversation in pairs. Then change the days and the times, and ask each other: What do you do on Saturdays?
Day 2: find someone who always gets up before six, never watches TV, or works at the weekend. Report back with he and she: Omar never watches TV.
Day 3: the rota task. Give each pair two different rotas. They find a day and a time to meet, and say it back to check.
Day 4: talk about the book, answer questions, and let two learners read about their weekday aloud.
